decisions.mark: explains that the health monitor does NOT invoke its status callback from the monitor thread — it queues events under a mutex and the caller drains them on its own thread
decisions.detail: QUOTE: "**Drain-then-dispatch.** `HealthMonitor::process_events` swaps the event queue out under `event_mutex_`, then invokes callbacks with the lock released. The callbacks run on the engine thread, not the monitor thread (`health_monitor.cpp:118`)." | WHY: The answer states that events are queued under a mutex, drained by process_events, and callbacks run on the caller's engine thread rather than the monitor thread. || QUOTE: **Drain-then-dispatch.** `HealthMonitor::process_events` swaps the event queue out under `event_mutex_`, then invokes callbacks with the lock released. The callbacks run on the engine thread, not the monitor thread (`health_monitor.cpp:118`). | WHY: The answer states that events are queued under `event_mutex_`, drained by `process_events`, and that callbacks run on the engine (caller) thread rather than the monitor thread. || QUOTE: "**Drain-then-dispatch.** `HealthMonitor::process_events` swaps the event queue out under `event_mutex_`, then invokes callbacks with the lock released. decisions.mark: identifies the cancellation observer thread as existing to bridge an atomic into a plain int, because the C ABI boundary cannot carry an atomic
decisions.detail: QUOTE: The cancel and interrupt flags are `std::atomic`, polled every 10 ms by the observer and poller threads. The C ABI carries only `int*`, so no atomic crosses the `.so` boundary (`response_generator.cpp:379`). | WHY: The answer says the observer/poller threads poll atomic flags and that the C ABI carries only `int*`, so no atomic can cross the boundary. That is the bridging rationale. || QUOTE: The cancel and interrupt flags are `std::atomic`, polled every 10 ms by the observer and poller threads.
